references.text: Earlier, Luke tells us that Jesus taught daily in the temple, which forms the direct context for the chief priests and scribes confronting him in 20:1. See [ref:Luk 19:47-48|Luke 19:47-48].

The parallel passage in Matthew where the chief priests and elders of the people come to Jesus while he is teaching in the temple and ask about his authority. See [ref:Matt 21:23-27|Matthew 21:23-27].
The parallel passage in Mark where the chief priests, scribes, and elders question Jesus about his authority. See [ref:Mark 11:27-33|Mark 11:27-33].

In John's Gospel, the high priest questions Jesus about his teaching and his disciples, showing the same pattern where religious leaders challenge Jesus' authority. See [ref:Joh 18:19-21|John 18:19-21].
Jesus proclaims the gospel (εὐαγγελιζομένου), linking back to his programmatic declaration in Nazareth where he states he is anointed to preach good news. See [ref:Luk 4:18-19|Luke 4:18-19].
Luke summarizes Jesus' daily teaching practice in the temple during this period, when people came early to hear him—the same situation described in 20:1. See [ref:Luk 21:37-38|Luke 21:37-38].
After Pentecost, Peter and John face a similar confrontation with the priests, the temple guard, and the Sadducees while teaching the people in the temple. See [ref:Apg 4:1-3|Acts 4:1-3].
The Jews demand a sign from Jesus as proof of his authority to act in the temple, reflecting the same question about authority. See [ref:Joh 2:18|John 2:18].

The priests and elders of Israel also confronted King Uzziah when he acted beyond his authority in the temple—an Old Testament example of religious leaders guarding the temple's authority. See [ref:2 Krøn 26:17-18|2 Chronicles 26:17-18].

The priests, prophets, and people seized Jeremiah while he was prophesying in the temple—a pattern where religious leaders challenge someone speaking with divine authority in the temple. See [ref:Jer 26:7-8|Jeremiah 26:7-8].
